title: Vital Signs
in30Seconds: Vital signs are the basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions — the body's way of reporting how it is running. The five measured in routine care are temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation. Adult reference ranges exist for each one, but 'normal' depends on age, health, and the individual. A single reading means little by itself; the baseline and the trend over time carry the message. Sudden changes are signals worth taking seriously.
whyItMatters: Every healthcare visit starts with vital signs because they are the fastest honest snapshot of how the body is running. A sudden change — a fever that appears, a pulse that climbs, an oxygen level that dips — is often the first clue that something is wrong, sometimes before the person feels any different. For students entering nursing and allied health, taking and interpreting vital signs is a daily skill and an early professional responsibility. For everyone else, understanding the basics makes you a better observer of your own body and a more informed partner in your own care.
learningObjectives: Define vital signs as the basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions, following the OpenStax nursing-textbook description.
Name the five vital signs — temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation — and state what each one measures.
Explain why adult reference ranges are only a guide and why 'normal' varies with age, health, and the individual.
Apply the baseline-and-trend idea to decide whether a single reading is concerning.
Analyze a change in a patient's vital signs and explain why it prompts checking and reporting.

collegeVersion.heading: A working definition
collegeVersion.body: Vital signs are the basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions. The OpenStax nursing textbooks describe them as markers of physiological homeostasis — the body's balanced, steady internal state — and as measurements essential for monitoring a patient's progress. MedlinePlus, the consumer health service of the U.S. National Library of Medicine, notes that vital signs reflect essential body functions, including heartbeat, breathing, temperature, and blood pressure. Two parts of that definition carry the weight. First, 'basic': these are quick, mostly painless measurements taken at the bedside or in the home, not laboratory tests that need blood or urine. Second, 'essential functions': each one reports on a system the body cannot do without — heat regulation, the heart's pumping, breathing, the pressure inside the arteries, and the oxygen reaching the blood.

collegeVersion.heading: The five measurements and what each one tells you
collegeVersion.body: Routine care measures five vital signs, and each one answers a single question about the body. Temperature measures how hot the body is — how well heat production and heat loss stay balanced; a climbing temperature often means the body is fighting something, such as an infection. Pulse, also called heart rate, counts the heartbeats per minute — how fast the heart is pumping. Respirations count the breaths per minute — how fast and how well the person is breathing. Blood pressure measures the force of blood against the artery walls — how hard the heart works to push blood and how much resistance the vessels offer. Oxygen saturation, or SpO2, estimates the percentage of hemoglobin that is carrying oxygen — how well oxygen is reaching the blood. Each of these five has its own full lesson in this course; here the point is the set. In practice the five are read together, because they are connected: a fast respiratory rate often pairs with a fast pulse, and falling oxygen saturation can show up alongside a falling blood pressure.

collegeVersion.heading: Reference ranges: real, but flexible
collegeVersion.body: Adults have reference ranges for each vital sign, and they are genuinely useful. For a resting adult, common textbook references are roughly: temperature 97–99°F (about 36–37°C) by mouth, pulse 60–100 beats per minute, respirations 12–20 per minute, blood pressure below 120/80 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 95–100 percent on room air. The honest note: these are guides for a healthy resting adult, not universal truths. MedlinePlus warns that normal vital signs change with age, sex, weight, exercise capability, and overall health. What is normal for a newborn — a resting heart rate around 130 — would be alarming in an adult. The same adult's numbers move with activity, anxiety, illness, and medication. A reference range tells you where most healthy adults sit; it does not tell you where this particular person sits.

collegeVersion.heading: Why they matter: changes are the message
collegeVersion.body: Vital signs matter most when they change. The OpenStax nursing text puts it plainly: changes such as a fever, a climbing heart rate, or a falling blood pressure are signs that the body is no longer in balance, and understanding these signs can help prevent a life-threatening emergency. Original example: Mei, age 62, is recovering at home after knee surgery. Her temperature has run about 98°F all week, and her resting pulse has stayed in the high 70s. On Thursday morning she feels warm; the thermometer reads 101.2°F and her pulse is 104. Either number alone sits near the edge of the adult ranges, but the change from her own baseline is the message — so she calls her care team, who ask her to come in. A urine test finds an infection and treatment starts the same day. The vital signs did not diagnose anything; they sounded the alarm early.

collegeVersion.heading: The practice: baseline, trends, and who measures them
collegeVersion.body: Vital signs are gathered on the first encounter with a patient to establish a baseline, then routinely afterward according to the person's condition and the facility's orders. What matters is the trend: a series of readings over time that maps what is normal for that particular patient. One reading is a snapshot; the trend is the story. Nurses are the professionals who obtain, validate, interpret, and document vital signs, and they use nursing judgment to recheck them whenever a patient's condition changes, even if the scheduled time has not arrived. Nursing assistants measure vital signs such as blood pressure and temperature as part of routine care and report changes to the nurse. Patient care technicians and medical assistants take them too, in hospitals and clinics. And with training, patients monitor vital signs at home — blood pressure cuffs and pulse oximeters are common household tools — which is why understanding the basics serves everyone, not just clinicians.

vocabulary.definition: The basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions — temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation.
A person's usual set of vital sign values, established at the first encounter and used as the comparison point later.
The pattern formed by a series of vital sign readings taken over time, showing what is normal for that individual.
A measurement of how hot the body is, reflecting the balance between heat production and heat loss.
The pressure wave felt in the arteries each time the heart beats; reported as the heart rate in beats per minute.
The breaths a person takes per minute, counted as part of the vital sign assessment.
The force of blood against the artery walls as the heart pumps, reported as two numbers such as 120/80.
An estimate, usually from a pulse oximeter, of the percentage of hemoglobin in the blood that is carrying oxygen.
The typical span of values seen in healthy adults, used as a guide rather than a hard rule for any one person.
The body's balanced, steady internal state, which vital signs help monitor and which illness can disturb.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Vital signs are the body's basic signals — quick measurements that tell you how the engine is running. There are five main ones: temperature (how hot), pulse (how fast the heart beats), respirations (how fast you breathe), blood pressure (how hard the blood pushes on the artery walls), and oxygen saturation (how much oxygen the blood is carrying). They get checked at almost every healthcare visit, partly to catch problems early and partly to build a record of what is normal for you. The numbers have typical adult ranges, but the range is a guide, not a verdict: what is normal for a newborn is not normal for an adult, and what is normal for you can differ from what is normal for your neighbor. A single reading tells you little; the change from your own usual numbers is what speaks.
eli10.analogy: Think of the check-engine light. The light does not tell you which part failed — it just says something under the hood is off, and you would not drive cross-country ignoring it. Vital signs work the same way. A temperature that climbs, a pulse that quickens, an oxygen level that drops: none of them names the problem, but each one says 'look under the hood now.' The person who knows their usual numbers — their baseline — is the one who notices when the light comes on.
eli10.analogyLimits: The comparison has limits. A check-engine light is a single warning, while vital signs are five gauges that are also useful when nothing is wrong: they build the baseline that makes the warning meaningful. And unlike a car, a person's numbers move for ordinary reasons — exercise, nerves, a hot day, a cold. A change is a prompt to check and ask, not an automatic emergency. The gauges also need a skilled reader: the same reading that is routine for one person can be a red flag for another, which is why trends, context, and a clinician's judgment complete the picture.

workedExample: Priya is a first-year nursing student on a medical-surgical unit. At 0700 she takes Mr. Delgado's vital signs: temperature 98.4°F, pulse 74, respirations 16, blood pressure 118/76, and oxygen saturation 98 percent. She checks his chart and sees that his numbers have run close to these all week — his baseline is stable. At 1300, after lunch, his nurse asks her to recheck him because he feels warm. Priya measures: temperature 100.1°F, pulse 92, respirations 20, blood pressure 124/80, and oxygen saturation 96 percent. Every number has moved away from the morning baseline. Priya does not diagnose anything — she documents the readings, reports the change to the nurse, and the nurse notifies the provider, who orders a urine sample that comes back positive for a urinary tract infection. The vital signs did not name the infection. They noticed it first.

commonMistakes.mistake: A single reading tells you everything you need to know.
commonMistakes.correction: One number means little on its own. Readings are gathered at the first encounter to build a baseline, and the trend over time is what shows whether this patient is stable or changing. A pulse of 96 is unremarkable for the general population but a clear change for a patient whose usual resting pulse is in the mid-60s.

Adult reference ranges are guides for a healthy resting adult. Normal varies across the life span — a newborn's resting heart rate of about 130 is expected, while the same number in an adult would be fast — and it also varies with health, fitness, medication, and the individual's own baseline.

commonMistakes.mistake: Vital signs are only checked when someone is sick.
commonMistakes.correction: Vital signs are taken routinely, including for healthy people, precisely so there is a baseline to compare against later. A baseline taken when someone is well is what makes a later change visible.

Nursing assistants, patient care technicians, and medical assistants measure vital signs as part of routine care in hospitals, clinics, and long-term care facilities. Nurses obtain, validate, interpret, and act on them, and people at home can be taught to measure their own.

commonMistakes.mistake: Any change in a vital sign is an emergency.
commonMistakes.correction: A change is a prompt to check, document, and report — not an automatic crisis. Ordinary factors such as activity, anxiety, a hot day, or a recent meal move the numbers, so the reader considers context and the trend before deciding how urgent the change is.

compareContrast.distinction: A baseline is this person's own usual values, built from their past readings. A reference range is the typical span for healthy adults in general. The baseline tells you what is normal for this patient; the range tells you where most adults sit. When the two disagree, the change from baseline usually carries more weight.

A single reading is a snapshot of one moment — useful, but easily affected by activity, anxiety, or equipment. A trend is the pattern of readings over time, which smooths out those bumps and reveals whether the body is stable, improving, or moving in a concerning direction.

Vital signs are quick bedside measurements that reflect the body's essential functions in real time — no needles, no waiting for a lab. Laboratory tests analyze samples of blood, urine, or other fluids and give deeper detail about specific substances or cells. Vitals raise the alarm; labs help explain what is behind it.

keyTakeaway: Vital signs are the body's basic signals: five quick measurements — temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation — that reflect how the essential systems are running. Adult reference ranges are a guide, but your own baseline and the trend over time carry the real message: sudden changes are the body's check-engine light.

questionBank.prompt: A nursing student is explaining vital signs to a family member visiting the unit. Which description matches how the OpenStax nursing textbooks define them?
options: Basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions and are used to monitor a patient's progress.
Laboratory tests that require a blood or urine sample.
Medications prescribed to control high blood pressure.
Insurance codes used to bill for a hospital stay.
questionBank.explanation: The OpenStax nursing texts describe vital signs as markers of the body's balanced state (homeostasis) that are essential for monitoring patient progress. They are bedside measurements, not lab tests, medications, or billing codes — which is what rules out the other three options.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the working definition of vital signs

questionBank.prompt: Mr. Kim's chart shows that his resting pulse usually sits in the mid-60s. During morning rounds, the nursing assistant measures his pulse at 96 beats per minute. What does this finding mean?
options: It is meaningless, because 96 is a perfectly normal adult pulse.
It is within the general adult range but a clear change from his baseline, so it should be checked further.
He is having a heart attack and needs emergency resuscitation right now.
The only possible explanation is that the equipment is broken.
questionBank.explanation: Ninety-six falls inside the adult reference range of 60–100, but the patient's own baseline is the mid-60s, and the change from baseline is what signals a possible problem. Dismissing it, assuming a heart attack without other evidence, or blaming the equipment all ignore the baseline-and-trend principle.
questionBank.skill: Applying baseline-versus-range reasoning to a pulse reading

questionBank.prompt: A patient care technician is listing the vital signs she will measure during her morning rounds. Which list contains all five standard vital signs?
options: Height, weight, body mass index, pain score, and appetite.
Pulse, blood pressure, pain score, temperature, and weight.
Temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation.
Heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, pain score, and height.
questionBank.explanation: The five vital signs in nursing practice are temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation. Height, weight, and body mass index are anthropometric measurements, and pain — sometimes called the sixth vital sign — is a separate assessment, which rules out the other lists.

questionBank.prompt: A father is worried because his newborn daughter's resting heart rate is 130 beats per minute, which he knows would be fast for an adult. What is the most accurate response?
options: A heart rate of 130 means she needs to see a cardiologist immediately.
All people, regardless of age, should have a resting heart rate between 60 and 100.
The monitor must be broken, because no healthy baby's heart beats that fast.
Newborns naturally have much faster heart rates — 130 is within the normal range for her age.
questionBank.explanation: Normal vital signs vary across the life span. A newborn's resting heart rate normally runs about 100–160 beats per minute, so 130 is expected for her age even though the same number would be fast for an adult. The other options treat the adult range as universal, which is exactly the mistake the age-variation idea corrects.
questionBank.skill: Applying age-based normal ranges to a vital sign reading

questionBank.prompt: During a home visit, a nurse checks Ms. Rivera, who is recovering from pneumonia. Compared with her last visit, her temperature has risen from 98.2°F to 100.6°F and her oxygen saturation has dropped from 97 percent to 93 percent. Which response best applies the 'changes are the message' idea?
options: No action is needed because both readings are close to the adult reference ranges.
Tell her to take a hot bath right away to bring the temperature down.
Document the change from her baseline and report it to the provider, since both numbers moved together in a concerning direction.
Assume the pulse oximeter is inaccurate because she is wearing nail polish.
questionBank.explanation: Both numbers moved away from this patient's own baseline in the same concerning direction — fever up, oxygen down — which is the classic signal to check, document, and report. Ignoring the change because the values are near ranges, giving unsafe advice, or blaming equipment without evidence all miss the message.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a change in vital signs against a patient's baseline

provenance.rightsStatus: reference-only sources (OpenStax nursing textbooks, MedlinePlus, BLS); no source prose adapted; all examples original
provenance.transformation: The OpenStax nursing-textbook descriptions of vital signs (markers of physiological homeostasis; the five measurements; reference ranges and their limits; baseline and trends; monitoring practice) and the MedlinePlus consumer definition were synthesized into an original lesson — working definition, five measurements, flexible ranges, why changes matter, and who measures them — with entirely original examples (Mei's fever after knee surgery; Priya's clinical day; Mr. Kim's pulse; the check-engine-light analogy).
